regional_origin: Tamil Sri Lanka (Northern and Eastern provinces)

ingredients.name: Chana dal (split chickpeas / kadala parippu)
ingredients.notes: about 1 cup; soaked overnight or for at least 4-5 hours; drain well before grinding

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.notes: medium, finely chopped; do not blend -- chopped onion gives the best texture

ingredients.name: Coriander leaves
ingredients.notes: finely chopped; optional but adds freshness

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.notes: to taste; chana dal absorbs salt well -- add more than you think

ingredients.name: Chickpea flour (besan) or all-purpose flour
ingredients.notes: optional binding agent; helps the vadai hold together if the mixture is too loose

steps.instruction: Soak the chana dal in plenty of cold water for at least 4-5 hours, or overnight. The dal should double in size and feel soft when pressed. Drain very thoroughly -- excess water makes the vadai absorb more oil during frying.

Set aside about 2-3 tablespoons of soaked dal whole. Transfer the rest to a food processor or grinder. Pulse to a coarse, slightly rough paste -- not smooth. There should be visible pieces of dal remaining. Transfer to a bowl and add the reserved whole dal pieces.

Add the chopped onion, green chillies, garlic, ginger, curry leaves, coriander leaves, fennel seeds, chilli powder, turmeric, and salt. Mix well with your hands until it forms a cohesive dough that holds its shape when pressed. If too loose, add chickpea flour 1 tablespoon at a time.
Divide the mixture into 12-15 portions. Wet your hands lightly with water. Roll each portion into a ball, then flatten into a disc about 1cm thick and 5cm across.
Heat the oil to 175C (350F). Test with a small piece of batter -- it should rise immediately without browning too fast.

Gently slide 3-4 vadais into the oil at a time. Fry over medium heat for 3-4 minutes per side, turning once, until deep golden and crispy on both sides. Do not crowd the pan or raise the heat -- medium heat allows the inside to cook through before the outside browns.
Drain on paper towels. Serve hot with coconut chutney, pol sambol, or tomato sauce. Masala vadai are at their best eaten immediately while hot and crispy.

source_site: islandsmile.org (kadala parippu vadai), cross-checked against kitchensimmer.com, theflavorbender.com, foodviva.com, swasthi's recipes, sharmispassions.com, vegrecipesofindia.com, and revisfoodography.com
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 8+ independent sources from both Sri Lankan and South Indian cuisines given the shared tradition; strong agreement on coarse grinding, keeping onion hand-chopped rather than blended, and medium frying heat
notes: Masala vadai (also called chana dal vada, paruppu vadai in Tamil, kadala parippu vadai in Sinhala) is shared across South Indian and Sri Lankan Tamil cuisine and is a staple tea-time snack across the Northern and Eastern provinces. It is distinct from ulundu vadai (sl_048), which uses urad dal and is soft inside with a doughnut hole; masala vadai uses chana dal, is flatter and disc-shaped, and is crispy and crunchy throughout. The coarse grind is essential -- a smooth paste makes dense, doughy vadai rather than the characteristically crunchy, textured result. Keeping the onion hand-chopped (not blended) is consistently recommended across all sources as it preserves texture and prevents excess moisture in the dough. The total_time_min includes the 2.5-hour soak period.
